---
title: "From linguistic records to probabilities"
---

Before we fit a statistical model, we must decide how to represent the observations. The same audio file might yield a table with one row per speaker, word, or vowel token. The same corpus might yield a table of documents, sentences, tokens, or lexical types. A statistical model can describe only the distinctions preserved in the resulting table.

This module develops that point in two stages. The first stage concerns linguistic records and numerical patterns. The second builds a probability model one object at a time.

## From records to comparisons

We begin with [turning linguistic records into data](linguistic-data.qmd). That page separates a stored record from the unit represented by one row. It also asks which identifiers repeat and which variation disappears during aggregation.

The next page turns [a research question into a comparison](making-sense-of-data.qmd). It specifies the response, the linguistic predictor, the observations being compared, and the estimand. These decisions state what a later numerical result is supposed to mean.

[Zipf's law](zipfs-law.qmd) supplies the first worked linguistic pattern. The rank and frequency calculation is simple enough to do by hand, but its interpretation is not. The example separates describing a curve from explaining why that curve appears.

## From possibilities to a probability model

We build a probability model in a fixed order. A [sample space](possibilities-and-events.qmd) specifies the possible outcomes. [Events](events.qmd) group those outcomes, and a [sigma-algebra](event-spaces.qmd) specifies which groups are measurable. We then construct [generated sigma-algebras](generating-event-spaces.qmd) and use a [probability measure](probability-measures.qmd) to assign probabilities.

The remaining pages ask how measurable events are related. [Mutually exclusive events](probability-concepts.qmd) cannot occur together. [Joint probability](joint-probability-of-events.qmd) assigns probability to an intersection, while [conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd) restricts attention to one event and rescales the probabilities within it. Once those ideas are in place, we can derive [the product rule](probability-factorization.qmd) and [Bayes' rule](bayes-rule.qmd), then define [independence](independence.qmd). Each page uses only concepts introduced on earlier pages.

## The representational question

For any linguistic dataset, keep asking the same question:

> Which represented outcomes and distinctions make this probability statement meaningful?

If we cannot answer this question, we may have done the arithmetic correctly without establishing what the result means linguistically. That is why we specify the representation before introducing more elaborate models.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) places this chapter within the full course. Begin with [turning linguistic records into data](linguistic-data.qmd).
